# Reverse Causation in Prediagnostic Studies

In a study that measures something in blood drawn before a cancer diagnosis, reverse causation means the disease affects the measurement rather than the measurement marking a risk or an early stage. A tumour already present, but not yet diagnosed, sheds DNA, provokes inflammation and changes metabolism. Any of these can make a marker look predictive when it is only detecting disease that already exists.

## Definition

The association between a baseline biomarker and later diagnosis is partly or wholly produced by preclinical disease at the time of sampling. It is a form of reverse causation in the usual epidemiological sense, specific to the time between sampling and diagnosis.

## Why it matters for us

For a cfDNA methylation marker the distinction is subtle, because detecting existing preclinical disease is exactly what an early-detection marker should do. The trouble is interpretation. A strong association driven by cases diagnosed within months of blood draw says little about how many years ahead the signal is useful, and nothing about risk. In the [[northvale-early-detection-study]] the 58 cases diagnosed within two years carry most of the signal, so the pooled estimate would mostly measure short-range detection.

For an exposure such as [[clonal-hematopoiesis]] in the [[ch-cancer-risk-analysis]], reverse causation would mean undiagnosed cancer (or its treatment, if a person had a prior cancer) drives clonal expansion. That is less likely but not impossible, and the same tools apply.

## How studies deal with it

- **Exclude early cases**: drop cases diagnosed within a fixed time after sampling (commonly 1 or 2 years) and see whether the association survives. Simple and widely understood; throws away information and the cut-off is arbitrary.
- **Stratify by time since sampling**: estimate the association separately in [[time-to-diagnosis-windows]]. A strong effect that fades with time is the signature of reverse causation or short [[lead-time]]; an effect stable across windows suggests a risk marker. This is the approach [[safizadeh-2026-inflammation-colorectal-reverse-causality]] uses for inflammation markers and colorectal cancer. [[rossides-2020-reverse-causation-nested-case-control]] takes a related route, testing how robust a nested case-control association is under assumed reverse causation bias.
- **Model time to diagnosis directly**, as in [[massi-2022-deep-survival-ewas-time-to-diagnosis]].
- **Use genetic instruments** where the exposure has them (Mendelian randomization), which removes the time ordering problem but answers a different question; see [[mendelian-randomization]].

## Our working rule

From the [[northvale-analysis-meeting-2026-06-24|2026-06-24 decision]]: exclude the first year from the main model, and always report every window. The detailed answer is in [[how-do-we-handle-reverse-causation-in-the-northvale-lead-time-analysis]].

## What it is not

- Not the same as [[lead-time]]. Lead time is the interval by which a signal precedes diagnosis; reverse causation is a threat to interpreting an association. Short lead time and reverse causation produce the same data pattern in a single-sample design and cannot be separated without repeated samples.
- Not confounding by a shared cause, although in practice both can be present.
